title: The palace of memory (10.8)
hookLine: memory is a vast palace, and God is found there
tomorrow: what if someone had been calling the whole time?

lines: A SONG, AND A WHOLE SUMMER.
cards: A song comes on in a store, and a whole summer comes back with it: the car, the heat, who was in the back seat. Augustine knew that door. He has just asked the sky about God, and the sky pointed past itself.
So where does he look next? Inward, into memory. People travel to marvel at mountains, waves, rivers and stars, he says, and walk right past themselves.

teach.h: THE FIELDS AND PALACES OF MEMORY.
teach.b: The question: where can a person find God after the sky says not here? Augustine's answer: in memory. In his Latin: et venio in campos et lata praetoria memoriae.
I come to the fields and spacious palaces of memory. Some things come the moment he calls. Some have to be fetched from hidden storerooms.
Some push forward uninvited, as if to say, maybe it's us you want? Inside are sky, earth and sea, colors in the dark, lilies told from violets without smelling a thing.
Further on he says that ever since he learned of God, God has stayed in his memory, and he finds God there whenever he remembers. Remembering as a way to God is shared ground with a neighbor.
In Islam, dhikr means remembrance of God, and the Qur'an says, in Pickthall's translation: "Verily in the remembrance of Allah do hearts find rest!"
It rhymes with the line Augustine opened the Confessions with: our heart is restless until it rests in you. Rest for the heart, found by remembering God, in two traditions' own words.

teach.h: SPOKEN PRAISE, OR A SEARCH WITHIN.
teach.b: One honest difference: in dhikr, Muslims repeat words of praise, aloud or quietly, alone or together.
Augustine's remembering here is a search, room by room, through his own mind, and he says God isn't there as one picture among the others.

how: Catholics practice remembering God's gifts in prayer, for example in the Ignatian examen, which looks back over the day for moments of grace.

games.q: what does “the palace of memory” mean?
o: a palace in Milan where Augustine taught
the mind's vast storerooms, where God is found
a trick for memorizing long speeches

games.q: the palace of memory — tap the pairs.

s: Augustine thought memory was small and easily emptied
he calls it fields and spacious palaces, holding sky, earth and sea.
the Qur'an says that in the remembrance of Allah hearts find rest
Augustine finds God in memory as one picture among the others
not as an image, he says; yet he finds God there whenever he remembers.

games.q: a Muslim teammate says she does dhikr before games, and asks if Catholics have anything like it. what's a fair answer?
o: Augustine found God by remembering too, though his was a search within.
nothing; Catholics don't remember God, they only read about him.
it's identical; every religion does exactly the same thing.
games.why: shared ground, honestly put: remembering God brings the heart rest in both traditions' words, and the practices differ: spoken praise in dhikr, a search through memory in Augustine.

practice: Walk back through your memory and count three graces from long ago on your fingers: a kindness, a rescue, a time someone held you up. Let each one come with its colors and sounds.
If you pray, you can give thanks for each, there in the room where you found it.

wordCard.voice: The palace of memory. Augustine's picture of the mind's vast storerooms, where he keeps finding God.

orig.note: Latin, Confessions 10.8: the spacious palaces of memory.

carryVoice: The fields of memory: what you've been given is still in there, waiting to be found again. Until tomorrow.

sources.q: et venio in campos et lata praetoria memoriae
Verily in the remembrance of Allah do hearts find rest!
